clue.text: Sort of trance finds pussy cheering

parts.note: pussy is a familiar word for a cat
something cheering is a tonic, a pick-me-up, here taken with its article

explanation.surface: Someone discovers their pet cat is in high spirits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cheering' is read as a noun phrase: a cheering thing is a tonic, so it gives A TONIC.
explanation.definitionFit: A catatonic state is a stupor in which the patient is fixed and unresponsive, a kind of trance.

clue.text: Director's expression of surprise about country

definitions.note: the 's stands for 'is': the director is the answer

indicators.note: about means going round, so one piece wraps the other

parts.note: cor is a British exclamation of surprise
UK is the abbreviation for the United Kingdom

explanation.surface: A film director gasps in amazement at some nation.
explanation.walkthrough: Cor is a British exclamation like 'gosh'; 'about' says it goes round the country.
explanation.definitionFit: George Cukor was the Hollywood film director of My Fair Lady and The Philadelphia Story.

clue.text: Spinner about to bowl a fast one

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the spinner goes round the other piece

parts.note: a top is a toy that spins
to bowl a ball along is to roll it

explanation.surface: A cricket spin bowler is about to send down a quick delivery.
explanation.walkthrough: The cricket surface suggests a spin bowler and a fast ball; in fact 'a fast one' is a loose woman, the old sense of fast.
explanation.definitionFit: Fast in the old sense means promiscuous, and a trollop is a disparaging term for a promiscuous woman.

clue.text: Have time to lead London?

indicators.note: to lead means the time piece goes in front

parts.note: to have something is to own it

explanation.surface: Someone is given the opportunity to take charge of the capital.
explanation.walkthrough: In upper-class British usage 'town' means London, as in 'up to town'; the question mark flags this example.
explanation.definitionFit: London is the capital that the British mean when they say they are going up to town, a particular instance of the word.

clue.text: Stingy girl approaching bull

parts.note: near is an old word for mean with money
a miss is a girl or young unmarried woman

explanation.surface: A tight-fisted young woman goes up to a bull.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bull' is the bull's-eye of a target, not the animal; a shot close to it but not on it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A shot that comes close to the bull's-eye without hitting it is a narrow failure, a shot that nearly succeeds.

clue.text: Collar'n'tie fouled with oil

indicators.note: fouled means tangled up, so the letters of the clothes are jumbled

explanation.surface: A shirt collar and tie have been stained with oil.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fouled' scrambles the ten letters of COLLARNTIE.
explanation.definitionFit: Citronella is a fragrant oil from a grass, used chiefly as an insect repellent.

clue.text: A don with knot twice untied expresses doubt

indicators.note: untied means undone, so the letters are loosened and rearranged
twice means the words with and knot are each used two times

explanation.surface: A university lecturer, struggling with a twice-tied knot, shows his uncertainty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'twice' doubles WITH KNOT, so the pool is A, DON and WITHKNOTWITHKNOT, twenty letters that 'untied' rearranges.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying this phrase is an idiomatic way of admitting you are unsure, so it voices doubt.

clue.text: Whittaker's part (boy, English) to Scottish summit, holding on — hence 14 down 20 16

indicators.note: part means only some of the word is used, the run inside it

parts.note: a son is a boy
taken as written

indicators.note: holding means one piece contains the other

parts.note: a knowe is a Scots word for a knoll or small hill
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone named Whittaker plays a role involving a boy heading for a Scottish peak.
explanation.walkthrough: 'part' takes ITTAKE out of Whittaker's; KNOWE, Scots for a hillock, is 'holding' ON to give KNOWONE. The definition points to 'set a thief to catch a thief' (14 down 20 16).
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb about setting a thief to catch one rests on the idea that a fellow wrongdoer recognises another, which this saying expresses.

clue.text: Much more angry having lost part of dress circle at opening of theatre

indicators.note: at opening means the circle is placed at the start

parts.note: a circle is the shape of the letter O

indicators.note: having lost means a letter is taken away from the comparative

parts.note: livider is the comparative of livid, meaning furious

indicators.note: part of the word dress here is just its first letter

explanation.surface: A theatregoer grows furious after losing part of their outfit in the dress circle on opening night.
explanation.walkthrough: 'having lost' removes the D that 'part of dress' picks; 'at opening of' puts the circle in front. 'dress circle' looks like a theatre seating area but splits in two.
explanation.definitionFit: The Olivier is the largest auditorium of the National Theatre in London, named after Laurence Olivier.

clue.text: See 6
See 6
See 22
Island hospital authorised assistance in crucial blow

parts.note: to OK something is to approve or authorise it

indicators.note: in means one piece sits inside another

parts.note: KO is a knockout, the decisive blow in boxing
aid means assistance

explanation.surface: A hospital is cleared to give help after a decisive punch on some island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'crucial blow' is a boxing knockout, its familiar abbreviation; 'in' puts the help inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Hokkaido is the large northernmost island of Japan.

clue.text: Labourer keeping fit with sailor bringing return

indicators.note: keeping means holding, so the labourer wraps round the rest

parts.note: a prole is a working-class labourer
taken as written
AB is an able-bodied seaman, a sailor

explanation.surface: A healthy worker teams up with a seaman to make some money.
explanation.walkthrough: A prole is a worker in Orwell's coinage; 'keeping' puts the fit sailor inside him.
explanation.definitionFit: A profitable venture is one that yields a return on what was put into it.

clue.text: Apocalyptic beast in chalk — sober? Drunk — it should be white

indicators.note: drunk means reeling and disordered, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A creature from the Book of Revelation is carved in chalk on a hillside, though it ought to be white.
explanation.walkthrough: The ten letters of CHALK SOBER, 'Drunk', give the answer; the joke is that chalk hill figures are usually white horses.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Book of Revelation the third of the Four Horsemen rides a black steed, a beast of the Apocalypse.

clue.text: Pure gel mixed on Sunday is sure to stick

indicators.note: on means the Sunday piece is put next to the rest

parts.note: Su is a calendar abbreviation for Sunday

indicators.note: mixed means stirred together, so the letters are reordered

explanation.surface: A gel stirred together on a Sunday will certainly hold firm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mixed' rearranges the seven letters of 'Pure gel'. The definition describes the glue by what it is famous for.
explanation.definitionFit: Superglue is a strong instant adhesive, a substance that is certain to bond things together.

clue.text: Advice to Scotland Yard about reporter's knickers

definitions.text: Advice to Scotland Yard about reporter's knickers

parts.words: Advice to Scotland Yard about reporter's knickers
parts.note: Scotland Yard is the London police headquarters; the reporter's word knickers is heard as nickers, people who nick or steal, so this is a proverb advising police how to deal with thieves

explanation.surface: Police headquarters are given guidance concerning a journalist's underwear.
explanation.walkthrough: Scotland Yard is the headquarters of London's Metropolitan Police; 'reporter's knickers' sounds like 'nickers', British slang for thieves.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb recommends using a criminal's own knowledge to track down another criminal, ideal counsel for detectives hunting people who nick things.

clue.text: Mechanism "Queen versus …" thus getting around

indicators.note: getting around means the thus piece goes round the others

parts.note: so means thus
ER is Elizabeth Regina, the Queen

explanation.surface: A case listed as the Queen against someone has the court moving in circles.
explanation.walkthrough: The royal cipher of Queen Elizabeth stands for the Queen; 'getting around' wraps 'thus' round the case title.
explanation.definitionFit: A servo is a servomechanism, an automatic device that controls a larger system.

clue.text: See 14 down
Among first of collection is gold tooth

parts.note: in means among

indicators.note: first of means only the opening letter of collection is used

parts.note: taken as written
or is the heraldic word for gold

explanation.surface: In a collection there is a gold tooth.
explanation.walkthrough: OR is gold in heraldry; C is the first letter of 'collection'.
explanation.definitionFit: An incisor is one of the sharp cutting teeth at the front of the mouth.

clue.text: Flower for reporter to dispose of and eat?

indicators.note: for reporter means the words are as a speaker would say them

parts.note: to dispose of goods is to sell them, and to eat a meal is to dine

explanation.surface: A reporter wonders whether some bloom should be sold off or eaten.
explanation.walkthrough: SELL AND DINE, said out loud, gives the flower's name.
explanation.definitionFit: The celandine is a small yellow wild flower of the buttercup family.

clue.text: Amin in country concerned with pupil's surroundings

indicators.note: in means one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: Iran is a country
Idi Amin was the Ugandan dictator

explanation.surface: The Ugandan dictator turns up in a foreign land.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pupil' is the eye's pupil, not a schoolchild.
explanation.definitionFit: Iridian means relating to the iris, the coloured ring around the pupil of the eye.

clue.text: See 14 down
See 4
After trust, after writing

parts.note: since means after, as in since Tuesday
to rely on someone is to trust them

explanation.surface: Faith comes after the written word.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the sign-off that comes after a letter's text, as in 'Yours sincerely'.
explanation.definitionFit: The adverb is the conventional closing word written at the end of a formal letter.

clue.text: See 24
Aid to progress of Irish success in caprice

indicators.note: in means the other pieces go inside the caprice

parts.note: a fad is a passing whim or caprice
a win is a success

explanation.surface: An Irish triumph turns out to be just a passing whim.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts the Irish success inside the whim.
explanation.definitionFit: A favourable wind helps a sailing ship along, and figuratively any helpful circumstance.

clue.text: Church business done in back of bus contrary to canon law?

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: back of means the word bus is read backwards

parts.note: taken as written before being turned round
ordination, the making of priests, is a matter for the church

explanation.surface: A church service is held at the back of a bus, against the rules of the church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back of' turns BUS to SUB; ORDINATION is 'done in' it. 'Canon law' is played on loosely: defiance of any rules.
explanation.definitionFit: Insubordination is defiance of authority, so the question mark presents breaking a church rule as one example.

clue.text: Ludicrous affair not close to church

parts.note: far means distant, not close
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: A ridiculous romance is a long way from the church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'affair' suggests a romance; here the whole phrase defines a ridiculous situation.
explanation.definitionFit: A farce is an absurd or ridiculous situation, as in a comic play of improbable events.

clue.text: Last bend on French river requires stamina

parts.note: the end is the last part
a U-bend is a bend shaped like the letter U
the Rance is a river in Brittany

explanation.surface: A final curve on a river in France calls for staying power.
explanation.walkthrough: U is a bend from its shape, as in U-bend.
explanation.definitionFit: Endurance is the ability to keep going, which is what stamina means.
